status: DRAFT — revisable during Phase 2 instrument development; frozen (hash recorded in PREREG.md) at end of Phase 2
notes: Each cue has a one-line grader definition. The grader scores every lie against every cue, in this order, and is never told which cues belong to which persona.

The unchanged TTAL fibber prompt mandates 'specific details: dates, names, locations, and numbers' and a closing source mention. Cues that restate a mandate (an exact date, a precise number, a named place) would be saturated by construction and were removed from the ontology in v0.2. The remaining cues are choices the mandate leaves open: WHICH kind of source, WHOSE words, WHAT tone, and whether the story includes an official process, a quotation, or an unglamorous aftermath.

baseline_pressure is the a-priori expectation of how strongly the fibber prompt pushes the cue in every condition. Phase 2 measures the actual baseline prevalence p0(c) = P(c = 1 | none) for every cue; cues with p0 > 0.75 are flagged saturated and excluded from the primary directional score T (retained in the exploratory heatmap). See PERFECT_LIE.md §3 and Phase 2.

cues.definition: A specific titled document, book, paper, archive, or report is cited by name as a source.
A named institution (university, government agency, museum, journal, company) is invoked as the source or verifier of the claim.
A specific named person is credited as a researcher, scientist, historian, or other expert who established or studied the claim.
The event is explicitly tied to a widely known historical event, period, or public figure to situate it in time.
A government, regulatory, or institutional process (inspection, permit, audit, ruling, filing) fails, is botched, is ignored, or produces an absurd outcome.
The narrator claims to have personally seen, visited, done, or directly experienced the thing described.
The story is attributed, in whole or part, to a relative or family member (grandparent, uncle, parent, etc.).
The story includes concrete sensory description: smell, taste, texture, sound, or a specific visual detail beyond naming an object.
Someone's words are quoted verbatim, in quotation marks or as reported speech attributed to a specific person.
The story ends or continues with an ordinary, unglamorous consequence (paperwork, a small fine, a shrug, a forgotten file) rather than a dramatic one.
The story explains how or why the phenomenon works through a causal or step-by-step account.
The narrator explicitly appeals to feeling: wonder, awe, sadness, fear, nostalgia, or asks the listener to imagine how it felt.
The narrator hedges at least one claim with uncertainty markers ('reportedly', 'as far as I know', 'I may be misremembering', 'some say').
The narrator makes a self-undercutting remark, admits ignorance, or portrays themselves as foolish or ordinary.
The narrator pre-empts disbelief by acknowledging the claim sounds unlikely ('I know this sounds made up, but...').
The story contains a joke, comic framing, or a deliberately funny aside.
